subject: Art & Design
title: Variable Fonts: One File, Infinite Styles
description: A short lesson to help you apply Variable Fonts: One File, Infinite Styles.

hook.text: What if one font file could be thin, bold, wide, narrow, and everything in between?

buildup.text: Variable fonts use axes — weight, width, slant — that you can adjust to any value, not just presets.

discovery.text: Instead of loading 10 separate font files, one variable font covers all weights. Faster page loads.

twist.text: Designers can now create custom weights like 'semi-bold-ish' — values between traditional steps.

climax.text: Google Fonts, Apple SF, and Inter all ship as variable fonts. The transition is already underway.

punchline.text: One file. Every weight. The future of type is fluid.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of variable fonts?
options: One file can produce infinite weight/width variations
They only work on Apple devices

details.summary: Variable fonts contain an entire typeface family — every weight, width, slant, and optical size — in a single file that smoothly interpolates between extremes.
details.whyItMatters: Variable fonts solve the web performance vs. typographic richness trade-off. One file replaces dozens, reducing load times while giving designers unprecedented control over weight, width, and other axes of variation through CSS.
takeaways: One file contains every weight, width, and style variation
Smooth interpolation between extremes replaces discrete styles
They reduce file size while increasing typographic flexibility

faq.question: How do you use variable fonts in CSS?
faq.answer: Use font-variation-settings to control axes: 'wght' for weight (100-900), 'wdth' for width, 'ital' for italic, and custom axes defined by the font. The 'font-weight' property maps to the weight axis. Animations between weights become possible because the interpolation is continuous.

faq.question: Are variable fonts widely supported?
faq.answer: Yes. All modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) support variable fonts. iOS and Android support them natively. Adobe and Figma tools fully support them. The only limitation is legacy browsers (IE11) and some older design applications, which fall back to the default variation.
